title: GLS Foundations, Part 1: Netlists, Cells and Liberty
description: What you actually simulate in gate-level simulation: how the netlist is built, how standard cells are described in Liberty and Verilog models, how timing violations become X, and why GLS needs more than one PVT corner.
content:
Gate-level simulation (GLS) has a reputation for being slow, painful to debug and full of X's. Much of that pain gets easier once you understand what sits underneath it: where the netlist comes from, how a standard cell is described, and how timing gets into the simulator.

This is Part 1 of a two-part series on GLS foundations for DV engineers. It covers the *what*: the netlist, the cells it's built from, and the files that describe them. Part 2 covers the *timing contract*: SDC, STA, reading timing reports, and getting your testbench ready for GLS.

Here's the big picture both parts keep coming back to:

```text
 Liberty (.lib) ─ cell speed per corner        SDC ─ timing intent (clocks, I/O, exceptions)
          \                                       /
           ──►  Synthesis → DFT → P&R → STA  ◄──
                              │
                Netlist + SDF (per corner)  ──►  GLS
```

---

## 01 — From RTL to the netlist you simulate

```text
RTL ──synth──► Netlist ──DFT──► Scan netlist ──P&R──► Routed netlist + SPEF ──STA──► SDF
   (Liberty, SDC)      (scan, MBIST, JTAG)   (CTS, buffering, sizing, ECO)
```

Every stage changes the design you'll eventually simulate:

| Stage | What changes | Why it matters for GLS |
|---|---|---|
| Synthesis | RTL is mapped to cells, logic is restructured, flops are merged or removed, names are flattened | Your RTL signal names may no longer exist, and synthesis–simulation mismatches show up here |
| DFT | Flops become scan flops, and MBIST and JTAG logic is added | Scan pins must be tied off in functional mode, and DFT GLS checks the scan chains |
| P&R | Clock tree, hold buffers, resizing and ECOs are added, and wire parasitics are extracted (SPEF) | Only the post-route netlist gives you real timing |
| STA | One delay per timing arc is calculated from Liberty and SPEF and written to the SDF | The SDF is what timing GLS back-annotates |

That's why GLS comes in more than one form, each run at a different point in the flow:

![Where each kind of GLS runs in the implementation flow](/blog/gls-p1-01-flow.png)

| GLS type | Netlist | What it checks |
|---|---|---|
| **Zero-delay** (functional) | Post-synthesis or post-DFT | Function on the real netlist: synthesis–simulation mismatches, X-propagation, inserted logic. No timing. |
| **Unit-delay** | Same | Like zero-delay, but every cell gets a tiny fixed delay (for example #1) to avoid race conditions between cells |
| **SDF timing** | Post-route | Real cell and wire delays plus timing checks (setup, hold, recovery, pulse width), at one corner per run |
| **DFT pattern simulation** | Post-DFT or post-route | Scan shift and capture, ATPG patterns before they go to the tester |

A sensible order is zero-delay first, so functional problems are fixed before you start debugging timing.

> [!NOTE]
> The netlist you simulate is not your RTL with different syntax. It's a different design that is *supposed* to be equivalent. GLS exists to check that "supposed to" under real conditions.

---

## 02 — Standard cells: the building blocks

A standard cell is a pre-designed, pre-characterized transistor layout for one logic function at one drive strength. All cells in a library share the same height so they can be placed side by side in rows.

Cell names encode a lot. Taking a sky130 example:

```text
sky130_fd_sc_hd__dfrtp_4
  fd = foundry · sc = standard cell · hd = high density
  dfrtp = D flip-flop, async reset, positive edge · _4 = drive strength
```

| Category | Examples | Why DV cares |
|---|---|---|
| Combinational | inv, nand2, a21oi, mux2, xor2 | X handling differs from RTL operators |
| Sequential | dfxtp, dfrtp (with reset), dlxtp (latch) | They carry the timing checks, and flops without reset start as X |
| Scan | sdfxtp (mux-D flop) | Added by DFT, so tie-offs matter |
| Clock | clkbuf, integrated clock gate (dlclkp, or sdlclkp with scan enable) | A glitch here corrupts everything downstream |
| Low-power | isolation, level shifter, retention | Checked in power-aware GLS |
| Physical | tap, decap, fill, diode | Present in the powered netlist, with no function |

The same cell is described several times, once for each tool that needs it:

![One standard cell, five views: DV engineers work with Liberty and the Verilog model](/blog/gls-p1-02-cell-views.png)

As a DV engineer you mostly deal with the last two. The library team produces the Liberty data through **characterization**: SPICE simulations of every cell across a grid of input slews and output loads, repeated at each PVT corner. The results are stored as tables, one `.lib` file per corner.

---

## 03 — Liberty: the cell's datasheet for tools

A Liberty file describes, for one PVT corner, what each cell does and how fast it does it.

```text
library (sky130_fd_sc_hd__ss_100C_1v60) {          /* one file = one PVT corner */
  time_unit : "1ns";
  cell (sky130_fd_sc_hd__nand2_1) {
    area : 3.75;
    pin (A) { direction : input; capacitance : 0.0024; }
    /* pin (B) omitted for brevity */
    pin (Y) {
      function : "!(A&B)";
      max_transition : 1.5;  max_capacitance : 0.08;
      timing () {
        related_pin  : "A";
        timing_sense : negative_unate;
        timing_type  : combinational;
        cell_rise (tbl) {
          index_1 ("0.01, 0.10");      /* input slew (ns)  */
          index_2 ("0.001, 0.010");    /* output load (pF) */
          values  ("0.050, 0.120", "0.080, 0.155");
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

The heart of the file is the **timing arc**: how a change on one pin affects another. Each arc type maps to something you'll see later in the Verilog model and in the SDF:

| Liberty timing_type | Meaning | Verilog specify | SDF |
|---|---|---|---|
| combinational | Input → output delay | `(A => Y)` | `IOPATH A Y` |
| rising_edge | Clock → Q | `(posedge CLK => (Q +: D))` | `IOPATH (posedge CLK) Q` |
| setup_rising / hold_rising | Setup and hold constraints | `$setuphold` | `SETUPHOLD` |
| recovery_rising / removal_rising | Async reset release vs clock | `$recrem` | `RECREM` |
| min_pulse_width | Minimum pulse width | `$width` | `WIDTH` |
| when: "B" | State-dependent delay | `if (B) (A => Y)` | `COND B (IOPATH ...)` |

A few details are worth knowing:

- **Timing sense** describes direction. Positive unate means the output follows the input (buffer, AND), negative unate means it inverts (inverter, NAND), and non-unate means it can go either way (XOR, mux select).
- **Setup and hold values can be negative.** The Verilog model has to handle that, as we'll see below.
- **Special attributes** mark cells for specific roles: `clock_gating_integrated_cell`, `is_isolation_cell`, `retention_cell`, `is_level_shifter`, `test_cell` and `dont_use`.

**How a delay is looked up.** The table gives delays only at grid points. For a real input slew of 0.055 ns and a load of 0.0055 pF, which sit halfway between the grid points on both axes, the tool interpolates between the four corners:

![Bilinear interpolation between the four nearest table points gives about 0.101 ns](/blog/gls-p1-03-liberty-lookup.png)

The output slew is looked up the same way and becomes the next cell's input slew. STA chains this calculation along every path.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The simulator never reads the `.lib`. STA calculates each delay once, for the real slews and loads in your layout, and freezes it in the SDF. GLS delays are only valid for the exact netlist and corner the SDF came from.

---

## 04 — Verilog cell models: how a cell behaves in simulation

A Verilog cell model has two parts: a **functional** part that describes what the cell does, and a **specify block** that describes timing. Here's a simplified sky130-style flop with async reset:

```verilog
`celldefine
module sky130_fd_sc_hd__dfrtp_1 (Q, CLK, D, RESET_B);
  reg  notifier;
  wire CLK_d, D_d, RESET_B_d;                 // delayed copies for negative checks
  not  (RESET, RESET_B_d);
  udp_dff$PR u_ff (buf_Q, D_d, CLK_d, RESET, notifier);   // UDP = behaviour
  buf  (Q, buf_Q);

`ifndef FUNCTIONAL                            // FUNCTIONAL → zero-delay GLS
  specify
    (posedge CLK => (Q +: D)) = (0, 0);       // placeholder, overwritten by SDF
    $setuphold(posedge CLK &&& RESET_B, posedge D, 0, 0, notifier,,, CLK_d, D_d);
    $recrem   (posedge RESET_B, posedge CLK, 0, 0, notifier,,, RESET_B_d, CLK_d);
    $width    (posedge CLK &&& RESET_B, 0, 0, notifier);
  endspecify
`endif
endmodule
`endcelldefine
```

What to take away from this model:

- **UDPs** (user-defined primitives) are truth tables. Any input combination that isn't listed produces X, which is where gate-level X-pessimism comes from.
- **`&&&` conditions** switch checks off while the flop is held in reset, so you don't get false violations during reset.
- **Negative timing checks** work by delaying D and CLK internally (`D_d`, `CLK_d`). Most simulators need a switch to enable this, for example `+neg_tchk` in VCS. Check your simulator's manual for the equivalent. Without it, negative limits become 0 and you'll see extra violations.
- **The default delays are zero.** If the SDF fails to annotate, your timing GLS silently turns into a zero-delay run. Always read the annotation log.
- **Power pins** (VPWR, VGND, VPB, VNB, enabled with `USE_POWER_PINS`) are needed for power-aware GLS. Also make sure the `` `timescale `` matches across the testbench, netlist and cell models.

### How a timing violation becomes an X

When D changes too close to the clock edge, `$setuphold` fails and toggles the notifier. The UDP has a row for "notifier changed", and that row drives Q to X. The X then spreads into every gate that Q feeds:

![D changes inside the setup window, the check fails, the notifier toggles and Q goes X](/blog/gls-p1-04-timing-violation.gif)

When you see a wall of X in a GLS waveform, trace it back to the *first* flop that went X, and check the simulator log for a timing violation on that flop at that time.

### How one number travels from Liberty into your waveform

Following a single clock-to-Q delay end to end ties sections 03 and 04 together:

![One clock-to-Q delay, from Liberty table to GLS waveform](/blog/gls-p1-05-delay-journey.png)

## 05 — PVT corners and why GLS needs more than one

One common misunderstanding: a Liberty file contains **no information about your design**. It only says how fast the library's cells are under one set of conditions. Timing specific to your design exists only after STA combines Liberty with your netlist and parasitics. So you get one `.lib`, one SDF, and one timing-GLS run per corner.

A corner is a combination of **P**rocess (slow, typical or fast transistors), **V**oltage and **T**emperature. A name like `ss_100C_1v60` means slow process, 100°C and 1.60 V. Between corners, the cells and functions stay the same and only the numbers change.

The same path can take very different amounts of time at each corner (illustrative numbers):

![The same path at three PVT corners (illustrative numbers)](/blog/gls-p1-06-pvt-corners.png)

| Corner | What it stresses | Bugs timing GLS finds |
|---|---|---|
| **SS**, low V, hot (max delay) | Setup | Late capture on deep logic, a late clock-gate enable, reset release (recovery) failures |
| **FF**, high V, cold (min delay) | Hold | Data racing through in the same cycle, glitches, races between testbench and DUT |
| TT (typical) | Nominal behaviour | A sanity check only |

Setup violations depend on frequency, so in silicon you can at least slow the clock. **Hold violations don't**: a hold failure means the chip fails at any speed. That's why FF-corner GLS deserves as much attention as SS.

SDF files store delays as `(min:typ:max)` triplets, and the simulator picks one with switches like `+mindelays` or `+maxdelays`. Make sure the delay selection matches the corner and check you intend, and record both for every run so results can be reproduced.

> [!TIP]
> At advanced process nodes, *temperature inversion* can make cold the slow case, so don't assume hot is always worst for setup.

---

## 06 — Key takeaways, tips and interview questions

### Key takeaways

- **The netlist is a different design.** It has been restructured, renamed, and extended with scan, clock-gating and power cells. RTL signal names may be gone.
- **Each cell has two descriptions you care about.** Liberty says how fast it is at one corner. The Verilog model says what it does and which timing checks apply.
- **STA connects them.** It reads Liberty, calculates real delays for your layout, and writes the SDF. The SDF fills the zeros in the Verilog specify blocks.
- **Timing violations become X** through the notifier and the UDP table, and that X spreads downstream.
- **One corner is never enough.** SS finds setup problems, FF finds hold problems, and hold failures can't be fixed by slowing the clock.

### Important notes

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Silent zero-delay runs.** If the SDF doesn't annotate, the specify blocks keep their default zeros and your "timing" GLS is really a zero-delay run. Always check the annotation log for errors and for how many entries were applied.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Same netlist, same corner, same SDF.** An SDF from an older netlist, or from a different corner than you think, gives results that look plausible but mean nothing.

> [!NOTE]
> **`FUNCTIONAL` and `+nospecify` switch timing off.** That's correct for zero-delay GLS and wrong for timing GLS. Keep separate, clearly named compile setups for each.

> [!NOTE]
> **Negative timing checks need to be enabled.** Without the simulator switch, negative setup or hold limits become 0 and you'll chase violations that don't exist.

### Practical tips

> [!TIP]
> Run **zero-delay GLS first**. Fix functional issues and X-propagation before adding timing.

- When you see a wall of X, **find the first X**, not the biggest one. Go back in time on the signal until you reach the flop or net where it started.
- **Read one real cell model** from your library, specify block and UDP included. It removes most of the mystery from GLS debug.
- Pick one flop and **trace one arc** through all three files: its `timing_type` in Liberty, its line in the specify block, and its entry in your SDF.
- **Keep a run log** for every timing GLS run: netlist version, SDF file, corner, min/typ/max selection, and simulator switches.
- Check that **non-reset flops** are expected to start as X, and decide deliberately how to initialize them rather than forcing everything to 0.

### Interview questions

**1. Why can't you just reuse RTL simulation results after synthesis?**
The netlist is a restructured design. Synthesis–simulation mismatches, X-optimism in RTL, and logic added later (scan, clock gating, power cells) mean RTL results don't automatically hold for the netlist.

**2. What's the difference between zero-delay, unit-delay and SDF timing GLS?**
Zero-delay checks function only. Unit-delay adds a tiny fixed delay to every cell to avoid races. SDF timing GLS uses real delays from STA and runs timing checks, one corner per run.

**3. What information does a Liberty file contain? Does it contain anything about your design?**
Cell functions, pin capacitances, delay and slew tables, setup and hold constraints, power and special attributes, all for one PVT corner. It contains nothing about your design.

**4. Does the simulator read the Liberty file?**
No. STA reads Liberty, calculates delays for your actual layout, and writes them to the SDF. The simulator reads the SDF.

**5. What's in a Verilog cell model's specify block?**
Path delays (such as `(posedge CLK => (Q +: D))`) and timing checks (`$setuphold`, `$recrem`, `$width`). The delay values are placeholders until the SDF overwrites them.

**6. How does a setup or hold violation turn into an X in GLS?**
The timing check fails and toggles the notifier register. The UDP has a row for a notifier change that drives the flop's output to X.

**7. What is a UDP, and why does it cause X-pessimism?**
A user-defined primitive is a truth table. Any input combination not listed in the table produces X, even in cases where real hardware would give a defined value.

**8. What does `timing_sense: negative_unate` mean?**
The output moves in the opposite direction to the input, like an inverter or NAND: a rising input causes a falling output.

**9. How does a tool compute a delay that isn't exactly on the Liberty table's grid?**
It interpolates between the nearest table points, using the actual input slew and output load.

**10. What are negative timing checks, and what happens if they're not enabled?**
Setup or hold limits that are negative, meaning data may change slightly on the other side of the clock edge. The simulator models them with internally delayed signals. Without the switch, the limits are set to 0, causing extra, false violations.

**11. Why do you need both SS and FF corners in timing GLS?**
SS has the longest delays and exposes setup problems. FF has the shortest delays and exposes hold problems. Passing at one corner says nothing about the other.

**12. Why are hold violations considered more dangerous than setup violations?**
Setup and capture happen on different clock edges, so slowing the clock can fix a setup failure. Hold is checked against the same edge, so it doesn't depend on frequency, and a hold failure in silicon can't be fixed by slowing the clock.

**13. Your timing GLS shows no delays at all. What do you check?**
Whether the design was compiled with `FUNCTIONAL` or `+nospecify`, whether `$sdf_annotate` ran, and the annotation log for errors such as wrong instance paths or mismatched arcs.

**14. What do `&&&` conditions in a timing check do?**
They make the check conditional, for example only checking setup and hold while the flop isn't held in reset, which avoids false violations.
